# Chapter 7 - sketch answers {.unnumbered}

\(1\) The IP address is personal data - an online identifier that can single
someone out. The order history linked to an email is personal data -
identifiable through the identifier. Fully anonymised statistics fall outside
the GDPR - provided no one can be re-identified. The health note is
special-category data (Art. 9), needing a stronger basis and tighter handling.
(2) Security answers only whether the data is safe, and the GDPR also asks
whether it may be processed at all. The database had no lawful basis under
Article 6, was never disclosed to the customers (failing transparency), and
exceeded any stated purpose (failing purpose limitation and minimisation).
Encrypting unlawful data does not make it lawful. (3) Controller: FastGoods,
which decides why and how. Processors: The cloud host and the courier (for
delivery data). Independent controller: The payment provider, which sets its own
purposes and means for the card transaction. Data subjects: The customers.
Article 28 requires a written data processing agreement binding each processor
to FastGoods' documented instructions. (4) Authority notification by Saturday
10:00 - 72 hours are hours, weekend included. Customers are told if the breach
is likely to result in a high risk to them (fraud or phishing exposure from
leaked contact and order data would qualify). Documentation is required for all
breaches (Art. 33(5)) so the not-reportable judgement can be defended in a later
inspection. (5) A database breach is a personal-data breach under the GDPR (72h
to Datatilsynet, Art. 34 to customers if high risk) and, for an in-scope entity,
a significant incident under a NIS-style regime (24--72--one month). The
preparedness plan of Lecture 12 - contacts, templates, decision-makers fixed
in advance - is what makes both clocks achievable.
